content.text: Modern LINACs didn't appear out of nowhere — treatment equipment evolved in stages, each one pushing toward deeper penetration, better skin sparing, and more clinical efficiency.
Gustav Bucky's tube; sits between X-ray and UV on the EM spectrum; used for superficial skin cancers
SSD 15–20 cm; cones collimate the beam, placed in contact with skin
SSD 50 cm; for years the most penetrating beam available; still used for skin lesions today
At 1 MV and above, equipment gains real depth penetration, better skin sparing, and clinical efficiency — several competing designs emerged before the linear accelerator became the standard:
First electrostatic generator to produce high-energy X-rays
Doughnut-shaped circular orbit; accelerates both electrons and photons
Two D-shaped magnets ("Dees") accelerate charged particles in an expanding spiral; foundation of proton therapy
Artificially activated Co-59 isotope in a double-welded steel capsule; the mainstay of external beam RT until the linear accelerator; first practical unit to penetrate below 0.5 cm skin depth
Which of these historical devices is the direct ancestor of modern proton therapy?
The cyclotron's dual-magnet, spiral-acceleration design is the foundation proton therapy machines still build on.

is the workhorse machine of external beam radiation therapy. It accelerates electrons to high energy and uses them to produce either a high-energy photon beam or an electron treatment beam, aimed precisely at a patient's tumor.
Early linear accelerators were large and bulky compared to today's machines, which are compact and fully computer-driven.
At a high level, a LINAC has four functional groups:
— the rotating structure housing the beam-generating and beam-shaping hardware, which rotates around the patient.
— houses supporting electronics and, on many machines, part of the waveguide and klystron/magnetron. The gantry rotates on bearings within the drive stand.
— the treatment couch (also called the "tabletop" or "patient support assembly"), which moves in multiple axes to position the patient at isocenter.
— where the therapist sets up and delivers the treatment, outside the treatment room.
, which functions as the cathode — a heated cathode that releases electrons via thermionic emission.
These electrons are injected into the
, a hollow, tube-like structure using radiofrequency electromagnetic radiation (microwaves) to accelerate them to nearly the speed of light. A
directs energy into the waveguide and prevents reflected microwaves from traveling backward.
Lower-energy machines (up to about 12 MeV) typically use a
(amplifier), which requires a separate low-power microwave source to amplify.
On most LINAC designs, the accelerated electron beam travels through the waveguide but needs to be redirected toward the patient. The
does this — redirecting electrons toward the exit window of the treatment head.

(commonly a 270° or "slalom" design) bends electrons of slightly different energies back to the same focal point, keeping the beam narrow and consistent despite small energy variations picked up in the waveguide.
What is the main purpose of the bending magnet?

options: To slow the electrons down before they hit the target
To redirect the electron beam toward the patient and refocus it
To produce the flattening of the beam profile

content.text: The bending magnet redirects the beam (often through 270°) toward the patient and refocuses electrons of slightly different energies to the same point.

pages.title: Treatment Head — Target and Flattening Filter

content.text: Once redirected, the electron beam either strikes a
(typically tungsten, a high-atomic-number material) to produce photons via
("braking radiation"), or the target is retracted and the electrons themselves are used directly for electron treatments.
For photon beams, the raw bremsstrahlung output is much more intense along the central axis than at the edges (forward-peaked). A
attenuates the center more than the edges to produce a uniform ("flat") beam profile across the field.
For electron treatments, both the target and flattening filter are moved
of the beam path, and a
to spread the narrow electron beam into a usable field.

pages.title: Ion Chambers — Dose and Symmetry Monitoring

content.text: Below the flattening filter sit sealed
(dose monitor chambers) that continuously measure beam output and symmetry in real time as the beam is delivered.

Two independent ion chambers provide redundancy — if the primary and secondary readings disagree beyond tolerance, the beam is automatically terminated. The ion chamber is what signals the machine to shut off once the requested dose (monitor units) has been delivered — a core radiation safety interlock, not just a dosimetry convenience.
The beam next passes through the
, a fixed conical opening that sets the
possible field size the machine can ever produce.

(the X and Y jaws) define the actual field size for a given treatment, within the limit set by the primary collimator. The jaws move to generate a customized field shape — this is covered in depth in the Field Size lesson.
Which collimator sets the absolute maximum field size the machine can physically produce?
The primary collimator is a fixed opening that sets the absolute maximum field size; the jaws then define the actual field within that limit.
Sitting below the secondary jaws is the
— covered in detail in its own lesson. Mechanically, it's simply the next beam-shaping layer in the head, after the jaws.
simulates the radiation field by illuminating the secondary collimator and MLC area, letting staff visually confirm field shape and position without turning on the actual beam.
rotates the entire treatment head around a horizontal axis, allowing the beam to enter the patient from virtually any angle in that plane.

(tabletop) moves independently in vertical, lateral, and longitudinal directions, and on many machines can also rotate. Together, gantry angle and couch position determine where the beam enters and where it's aimed.

is the fixed point in space where the central axis of the beam passes regardless of gantry angle — typically 100 cm from the source. Aligning the tumor to isocenter is the entire point of simulation and setup.

pages.title: Imaging Systems — OBI, EPID, and CBCT

content.text: Modern LINACs carry onboard imaging to verify patient position before (and sometimes during) treatment: the kV imaging device (On-Board Imager) and the Electronic Portal Imaging Device (EPID), which replaced film with silicon imaging technology reviewed immediately online. Both are covered in depth in the Image Production lesson.

pages.title: The Control Console and Modulator Cabinet

content.text: was developed specifically to reduce the risk of treatment errors, allowing verification of setup parameters before beam-on. The
houses the pulsed power supply and supporting electronics that drive the whole accelerator.
Safety systems built around the console and treatment room — interlocks, emergency-off controls, warning lights — are covered in depth in the Console Operations & Interlocks lesson.

pages.title: Medical Accelerator Hazards and Safety Considerations

content.text: A LINAC has many layered safety interlocks that stop the beam or prevent it from starting if a condition isn't met — door interlocks, collision-avoidance sensors, dose-rate and symmetry checks from the ion chambers, and more. Any one of these tripping halts treatment immediately.

You've now covered the full beam path: electron gun → waveguide → bending magnet → target/flattening filter → ion chambers → collimation (primary, jaws, MLC) → gantry/couch/isocenter → imaging → safety interlocks — plus the equipment history leading up to it.
